**Different amounts of time**

A mayfly lives briefly in a way that's hard to hold in your head. Many adults get twenty-four hours. Some get less: the females of certain species, which don't eat and don't molt again, have on the order of five minutes. They rise off the water, join the swarm, mate, drop their eggs, and finish—everything they will ever do compressed into an interval short enough to miss if you glance away to refill your cup.

A hummingbird, by contrast, burns through time like fuel. Its heart can exceed a thousand beats per minute, and its vision is fast enough that flowers and feeders alike seem to drift past in slow motion. Small, hot-blooded animals apparently take in reality at a higher frame rate; a day must unfold for them the way an hour does for us.

Then there are the deliberates. The Greenland shark patrols cold northern depths so slowly, and grows so patiently, that it may not reach maturity until it is around 150 years old. Some individuals alive today were probably swimming before the United States existed. And on dry granite slopes in California's White Mountains grows a bristlecone pine called Methuselah, which germinated around 2800 BCE—meaning it was already a quarter of a millennium old when workers were fitting the final stones onto the Great Pyramid. It is a living thing that watched the invention of writing spread across the world from a position of dignified seniority.

These creatures still operate on timescales we can roughly imagine. But tilt the picture further. Sharks have existed for something like 450 million years—tens of millions of years before the first true forests stood on Earth. Stranger still: recent measurements from the Cassini mission hint that Saturn's spectacular rings may be geologically young, perhaps only a few hundred million years old, possibly much less. If those estimates hold, sharks are older than Saturn's rings. Read that twice. Rings look eternal; sharks look familiar. Our instincts have it backwards.

Go deeper and the clocks get wilder. Tiny zircon crystals found in Australian sandstone crystallized 4.4 billion years ago and simply kept the date, each grain a sealed envelope from the planet's childhood. Meanwhile, at the opposite pole of duration, relativity quietly erases time altogether: the faster you move, the shorter your journey measures, and in the limit of lightspeed, departure and arrival collapse into the same instant. Nothing made of matter can ever ride a beam of light, but physics is fairly blunt about what it would mean to—an existence with no duration whatsoever. Zero time, start to finish.

So the spectrum runs like this: at one end, five minutes containing a whole biography; at the other, an entire universe's history compressed into a flash. And we sit in the unremarkable middle, with nervous systems tuned to decades and seasons, always slightly astonished that everything else refuses to tick along with us.

Here is the part I find most consoling. Any individual mayfly is a candle stub. But mayflies as a lineage have been doing this same elegant trick for roughly three hundred million years—they predate the dinosaurs, and they'll likely outlast the trends of this era too. From the inside, its day is everything. From the outside, the whole glittering dynasty is one long continuous shimmer that shows no sign of stopping.

Duration, it turns out, depends entirely on who's asking. Tonight, somewhere warm, a mayfly is living out all of its allotted brightness in a single golden hour—while far away, light is arriving at its destination at exactly the same moment it departed, having spent eons crossing the dark.

- Greenland shark longevity: Nature 2016 Nielsen et al.: 392 ± 120 max; sexual maturity female ~156 ± 13. Good: "reach sexual maturity around one hundred fifty" and "one specimen born possibly ~1600s?" 272 yr old typical—born ~1745ish. Born before US declaration (1776)? 392 -> 1624. - Bristlecone Methuselah: germinated pre-2833 BCE (per Schulman); older than Great Pyramid completion by centuries. Statement fine.

Phrase: "a growing minority of evidence hints"; better neutral: "recent analyses suggest the main rings may be only 100–400 million years old—possibly less." Then: sharks win either way (450>400). "It is entirely possible...that sharks are older than Saturn's rings."

- Ephemeroptera antiquity: stem-group mayflies Carboniferous (~330 Ma?) definitive Permian ~299-252. "roughly three hundred million years." Safe: "on the order of three hundred million years."

- Photon proper-time caveat handled via limiting argument; explicitly note you can't actually sit on a photon (rest frame undefined), use "in the limit."

Good. Now compose with stylistic care. Also ensure no opening with "I". Begin with mayfly image—strong hook.

One more consideration: should I add a brief preamble to the user ("Here's a short essay...")? My guidelines say no unnecessary throat-clearing; jumping straight into the piece with a title reads cleanest. Perhaps no meta commentary at all—or a tiny one-line lead-in? Straight-in feels right for "write freely."

Final polish targets: avoid repeated "consider/imagine"; vary verbs; check commas/dashes tasteful; end resonant not preachy.

Write final now.
